title: The longest day
description: Boss day. Multiple coordinated attacks at once, an unstable system, and at least once, the right answer isn't the most obvious one.

events.message: The internet is slow today — it looks like the network is under unusual load.
The screen freezes for a moment. It might be a side effect of the ongoing attack.
'The audit arrived TODAY, I need the compliance report NOW or we'll have serious problems.' — urgent message from management.

emails.subject: Invoice 4102 - our provider's new email server
emails.bodyHtml:
Dear all,

We migrated our email provider last week, so this email might get flagged as suspicious by your filter. Please find attached invoice 4102 for this month's maintenance services.

internalDbRecord.notes: Vendor active for 3 years. No history of security issues.

outOfBandCheck.channelDescription: Call to Vendor ABC's already-known finance contact
outOfBandCheck.details: The vendor confirmed by phone that they really did migrate email providers last week and that the invoice is genuine.

investigationHints.summaryText: SPF came back neutral because of the new relay server, but DKIM and DMARC are still valid and the routing reaches the vendor's real server.
The attachment is a real PDF, with no disguise or double extension.
The vendor confirmed by phone that they recently migrated email providers — that's exactly what's triggering the alerts.

explanation.short: Suspicious signs with a real explanation — not every yellow flag is an attack.
explanation.detailed: One of the email's checks came back neutral and it left a server that isn't the usual one — which would look suspicious. But there's a real explanation (an email provider change), confirmed by phone. The rest of the checks are fine, the attachment is clean, and the confirmation through another channel closes the case. After so many hacked vendors, it's tempting to report out of caution. But that also has a cost: it delays real payments and floods IT with false alarms. Investigating properly, here, means recognizing when everything is fine.

emails.subject: Urgent audio from the director - listen before you act
emails.bodyHtml:
Attached is the audio that director Ricardo recorded in the car on the way to the airport, asking you to temporarily disable the branch firewall so the external audit team can access it remotely today.

Audio file attached, 0:38.

internalDbRecord.notes: Domain registered 3 days ago. No 'Executive Office' sends security requests by email.

outOfBandCheck.channelDescription: Call to Director Ricardo Almeida's registered extension
outOfBandCheck.details: The director confirmed that he didn't record any audio and would never ask to disable the firewall by email.

investigationHints.summaryText: 'urgent_director_audio.mp3.exe' uses a double extension — it's not an audio file, it's an executable.
In the sandbox, the file attempts to connect to a suspicious external host.
The real director, contacted by phone, denied recording any audio or making this request.

explanation.short: A request to disable a security control, disguised as an urgent audio message from the director.
explanation.detailed: The request should already set off the alarm: turning off the network's protection because of an email is the kind of decision that can never rely on an urgent message alone. The 'audio' is actually a disguised program; the sender's address is recent and mimics the executive office's name; and the test confirms it's dangerous. A request to turn off security protection always requires confirming through more than one channel — never just what's written in the suspicious email itself.

emails.subject: Reminder: mandatory security training due by Friday
emails.bodyHtml:
Hello,

This is an automatic reminder that the annual information security training must be completed by Friday. Access it through the usual internal portal, under the 'Training' tab.

internalDbRecord.notes: Company's official domain, a recurring HR communication.

investigationHints.summaryText: It comes from the company's official address, with no links or attachments.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass — origin confirmed as legitimate.

explanation.short: Internal HR communication, with no links, no artificial urgency, no attachments.
explanation.detailed: After so many elaborate attacks, it's worth remembering: most everyday emails are normal. This one doesn't ask for anything unusual, has no attachment or external link, and comes from a confirmed address. Distrusting every email as if it were an attack also has a cost. The idea is to recognize the pattern, not to distrust everything.

emails.subject: Review of the salary adjustment spreadsheet - just between us
emails.bodyHtml: Hi! I saw that you work with Camila in finance. She gave me your contact and asked me to send you this team salary adjustment spreadsheet for you to take a look before we go to management. It's still very confidential, please don't mention it to anyone.

internalDbRecord.notes: No HR consulting firm with this name is registered as an active partner of the company.

investigationHints.summaryText: The spreadsheet contains enabled macros — a classic vector for executing malicious code.
In the sandbox, the file modifies a registry key used to automatically run programs when the computer starts.
There is no active partnership with this consulting firm — the name and context (Camila from finance) were invented to seem familiar.

explanation.short: A tailored scam: name-drops a real coworker to gain trust, with a dangerous spreadsheet.
explanation.detailed: This is a tailored attack: the scammer researched real company details (the name of a coworker in finance) to look real and ask for secrecy — which also stops the victim from checking with anyone else. The attachment is a spreadsheet that, when opened, asks you to 'enable content': that's when the dangerous program runs. The test confirms it installs itself to run every time the computer starts.

emails.subject: Legal notice - case no. 0834521-77.2026.8.26.0100
emails.bodyHtml:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Leroy Merlin is hereby notified to present a defense in the attached case within 15 days, under penalty of default judgment.

Access the attached official document for more details.

sandboxResult.details: The file attempted to encrypt files across multiple folders as soon as it was executed, including network shares.

internalDbRecord.notes: Real courts of justice do not notify companies by email with executable attachments — the official domain is '.jus.br'.

investigationHints.summaryText: 'tjsp-processos.org' is not an official court domain — real Judiciary domains use '.jus.br'.
'lawsuit_notice_0834521.pdf.exe' uses a double extension — it's an executable, not a document.
In the sandbox, the file attempts to encrypt files across multiple folders, including network shares — ransomware with the potential to spread.

explanation.short: Fake court notice using fear of a lawsuit to install a virus that locks your files.
explanation.detailed: This scam uses the fear of legal trouble to get you to open the attachment without thinking. The address imitates a real court, but official Brazilian court sites use '.jus.br' — never '.org'. The attachment hides a disguised program, and the test shows it's a virus that locks your files and demands money, able to spread across the company's network.

emails.subject: Final notice - pending PIX payment for the maintenance contract
emails.bodyHtml:
Dear all,

This is our final attempt to reach you before we suspend the maintenance contract. Please make the PIX payment of R$12,400 for the last 2 outstanding invoices to the key below today.

PIX key: 28.410.manutencao@quickpay.com.br

internalDbRecord.notes: Real vendor, but the maintenance contract has always been paid via invoice, never by PIX.

outOfBandCheck.channelDescription: Call to Vendor ABC's already-known finance contact
outOfBandCheck.details: The vendor confirmed that they did not send this charge and always get paid via invoice — their email account was compromised again.

investigationHints.summaryText: This vendor has always been paid via invoice — never by PIX. A change in payment method is a red flag.
The vendor confirmed by phone that they did not send this charge and that their account was compromised again.

explanation.short: The vendor's same real account, compromised again — the change in payment method gives away the fraud.
explanation.detailed: After email 1 from this same day (where a server change had a legitimate explanation), it's tempting to accept anything coming from this vendor without checking again — but every email needs to be evaluated on its own. Here, the strongest signal isn't technical, it's behavioral: this contract has always been paid via invoice, and now they're asking for PIX, with the urgency of a 'final notice.' The phone confirmation reveals it's the same previously compromised account, attacking again with a different pretext.
